scenario.name: Break Escape SAFETYNET: Mission 10 — Full Disclosure VMs
scenario.author: Z. Cliffe Schreuders
scenario.description:
# Break Escape SAFETYNET Mission 10: Full Disclosure
Virtual machines for the Break Escape SAFETYNET mission 10 narrative experience. Task Force Null goes into Tomb Gamma, a Cold War bunker in Montana, the night before the Publication. The operatives enter through the bunker's security monitoring host, which the camera and door systems report to. Its staging copy of the schedule lists the release channels, the cells' early-access orders and the first entries by city. The climax is in the release host and the core host, where each operative has to leave a confined service before reaching the machine beneath it.
## Included Systems
**bunker_monitor** (entry stage) - Debian 12 desktop system - Hosts a network traffic monitoring and threat-intelligence platform on a fixed port, with an unauthenticated command injection flaw in its login handler - The monitoring platform's service account (`secmon`) holds flag 1, reached through the command-injection foothold - A separate, password-gated staging account (`staging`) holds flag 2 and the staging copy of the release schedule in its own home, not readable from the flag-1 foothold
**release_host** (climax stage one) - Debian 12 desktop system - Runs the release service inside a privileged container, behind a bind shell on a random port - Two generated operative accounts. Neither is an administrator. The shell is a container, not the host. - Root's home on the host beneath the container holds flag 3 and the release service's arming / kill configuration (how six o'clock is armed and what stops it; the trigger itself is on the core console). The container itself holds no flag. - The shift operator's home holds the handover log, which names the port the release service's bind shell listens on
**core_host** (climax stage two) - Debian 12 desktop system - Runs a bind shell on a random port that drops into an older chroot jail - Root's home on the host beneath the jail holds a sealed archive addressed to the agent, holding flag 4 and a short note, opened only with the core access code the envelope on the desk carries. The stolen copy of the database and the live line into the Citadel's vault are here too. The jail itself holds no flag.
**attack_vm** - Kali Linux penetration testing platform - HaX's field console (SAFETYNET kit), racked at the gate, in the server hall and in the core; the only attack box
## Flags
Flag 1 and flag 2 are submitted at the forward post's terminal and the server-hall console. Flag 3 is submitted at the sealed section's hatch in the server hall. Flag 4 is submitted at the core host terminal, after the clock is stopped.
## Integration with Break Escape
These VMs are provisioned by the Break Escape game engine via SecGen integration. Players interact with these systems through the game's narrative and task system, with guided hints delivered via SAFETYNET field guides.
## CyBOK Coverage
- Command injection in web-facing services - Container and chroot confinement, and escaping them - Network mapping and service fingerprinting - Authorisation, least privilege and root access - Kill chains across a multi-stage intrusion

CyBOK.keyword: Application-based access controls: user-based access controls insufficiently limit privileges
Vulnerabilities and attacks on sandboxing misconfigurations

THE PUBLICATION. RELEASE SCHEDULE, STAGING COPY. 92,460 entries, with working detail. Fallback: 06:00 UTC, day 13, city by city. Key: all cities, one minute.
CHANNELS 1. Release servers, this site. 2. Trojan Horse backdoor. 47 million systems. Queued batch: Seattle.
EARLY ACCESS, 04:00 UTC. Two shares, paid for the theft. Zero Day. Collecting on site. Resale not permitted. Ransomware Incorporated. Collecting by its own arrangement.
FIRST ENTRIES. SEATTLE. 0001 Infusion pumps, a hospital group. The same flaw is live in 140 hospitals. SAFETYNET disposition: RETAIN. Operational value. Catalogued three years ago. 0002 Dispatch software. One county's emergency calls. 0003 Water treatment controllers, a city utility. End of life. The vendor cannot fix them.

RELEASE SERVICE. HANDOVER LOG. NIGHT SHIFT, DAY 12-13. The service runs in its container. Don't touch the host under it. The arming state is on the host. The trigger is on the core console, not here. Sign below at handover. relops 22:00 signed on. Release service listens on port:

RELEASE SERVICE. ARMING / KILL CONFIGURATION.
The publication is armed to release at 06:00 UTC, day 13, city by city, from the release servers on this site. The early-access shares go two hours ahead, at 04:00 UTC.
What stops it: - The release is held on a single trigger. Nothing goes until the trigger is thrown. - The trigger is on the core host's console, not on this host. This host holds the schedule and the arming state only; it cannot throw or cancel the release itself. - A full stop needs the core console. The key is one hand, one of theirs.
Staged by the release operators. The shift is on the operators' duty sheet.

VENDOR NOTICE. ALBION / CARROW CONTROLS. DRAFT. NOT SENT.
To: Carrow Controls, product security. Re: remote-management module, RM-4 series.
A flaw in the RM-4 remote-management module lets an unauthenticated operator take control of connected plant equipment. It is present across roughly four hundred UK sites, including the Albion plant. We have held it since 2017.
This notice was drafted so the vendor could issue a fix. It was never sent. SAFETYNET disposition at the time: retain for operational value.
Drafted 2017. Held. Not sent.

FOR THE AGENT. FROM A.T.
You came down through my walls. I built them to be come through, by someone who would read what was behind them. Everything on this box is true. The notice is real. I wrote it in 2017 and was told to hold it. The trigger is on my console. Come and talk to me before you touch it.
